_meta.title: DBAS-16 (Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep) · Sleep-Specific Cognitive Reframes
_meta.source: Morin, C. M., Vallières, A., & Ivers, H. (2007). Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep (DBAS): Validation of a brief version (DBAS-16). Sleep, 30(11), 1547-1554.
_meta.license: Items themselves are reportable peer-reviewed clinical instruments; paraphrased reframes are project-licensed.
_meta.note: 16 sleep-specific dysfunctional beliefs, complementary to the general cognitive_distortions library. AI should prefer matching against DBAS first for sleep-context, then fall back to general distortions.

dbas_items.belief: I need 8 hours of sleep to function the next day.
dbas_items.reframe: Sleep needs vary widely — anywhere from 4 to 10 hours can be normal. Quality matters more than duration, and daytime functioning is a better signal than hours.
dbas_items.socratic_question: If you only slept six hours but felt clear during the day, would that count as enough?

dbas_items.belief: If I sleep badly tonight I won't be able to function tomorrow.
dbas_items.reframe: One bad night makes tomorrow harder, but doesn't strip your abilities. Research shows when people feel they slept badly, their actual performance is only mildly affected.
dbas_items.socratic_question: Think back to days after bad nights — did you really get nothing done, or did you get through tired and still finish?

dbas_items.belief: Chronic insomnia will seriously damage my health.
dbas_items.reframe: Occasional sleep loss has no major long-term effects. Chronic insomnia does carry risk, but it's modifiable through behavioral therapy like CBT-I — and anxiety about sleep is itself more harmful than the sleep loss.
dbas_items.socratic_question: If insomnia really caused fast damage, sleep clinic patients would be much sicker. Many live and work normally for years. What does that tell us?

dbas_items.belief: I worry I've lost the ability to sleep.
dbas_items.reframe: Sleep is an automatic physiological process, not a skill. You don't 'forget' how. The more you try to control it, the harder it gets — letting go is itself what lets sleep come.
dbas_items.socratic_question: Do you have to think about how to breathe? Sleep is similar — it returns when you stop reaching for it.

dbas_items.belief: Bad sleep ruins my mood and makes me irritable.
dbas_items.reframe: Sleep does affect mood — but anxiety and worry also make you read your mood as 'because of bad sleep'. The two are bidirectional, not one-way.
dbas_items.socratic_question: How much of today's irritability is really from last night — and how much from things still bothering you?

dbas_items.belief: Medication is the only reliable way to deal with insomnia.
dbas_items.reframe: AASM and ACP guidelines list cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-I) as **first-line** treatment for adult chronic insomnia — comparable to medication in effect and without dependence risk. Medication is for short-term/acute use; behavioral therapy is preferred long-term.
dbas_items.socratic_question: If only meds worked, why would every major guideline put CBT-I first?

dbas_items.belief: I should be able to avoid, control, or predict insomnia.
dbas_items.reframe: Sleep is like weather — you can create good conditions but can't force it. Trying to 'definitely sleep tonight' activates alertness systems and backfires.
dbas_items.socratic_question: Last time you tried hardest to sleep, did control help — or do the opposite?

dbas_items.belief: A drink helps me fall asleep.
dbas_items.reframe: Alcohol does make you drowsy but disrupts deep sleep and REM, leading to mid-night wakings and early waking — worsening insomnia overall. There are dependence and health risks too.
dbas_items.socratic_question: After a drink to sleep, how's the back half of your night?

dbas_items.belief: I can make up for lost sleep on the weekend or later.
dbas_items.reframe: Sleep doesn't 'bank'. Catching up and sleeping in disrupt circadian rhythm and make the next few days harder. A fixed wake time is core to SRT (Sleep Restriction Therapy).
dbas_items.socratic_question: After sleeping in until noon Saturday, can you fall asleep Sunday night as easily as usual?

dbas_items.belief: Tired and unfocused today? It's because I slept badly.
dbas_items.reframe: Pinning everything on sleep strengthens sleep anxiety (makes sleep a 'threat'). Stress, diet, exercise, and mood all contribute to daytime feeling — sleep is one piece.
dbas_items.socratic_question: If you listed the 3 things shaping how you feel today, how many actually have nothing to do with sleep?

dbas_items.belief: I can tell whether tonight will be a good or bad night.
dbas_items.reframe: Predictions become self-fulfilling — expecting 'tonight will be bad' triggers alertness and disrupts sleep. Each night is independent; don't play yesterday's script tonight.
dbas_items.socratic_question: Last time you predicted insomnia and got it — was the prediction right, or did it cause it?

dbas_items.belief: My insomnia must be from a chemical imbalance.
dbas_items.reframe: Most chronic insomnia is maintained by behavior, cognition, and emotion (the 3P model). Even when physiological triggers exist, behavioral therapy is still first-line. Framing it purely as 'biology' makes people give up the parts they can change.
dbas_items.socratic_question: If it were purely chemical, why does adjusting routines and thoughts work for so many people?

dbas_items.belief: I need to cut down on daytime activities so I have energy to handle insomnia.
dbas_items.reframe: Less daytime activity → less energy expenditure → lower sleep drive → harder to sleep. Maintaining activity (especially regular exercise + sun) is key to CBT-I.
dbas_items.socratic_question: When you cut activities back, did sleep actually improve — or get worse?

dbas_items.belief: Bad sleep makes me worry about everything, and the worry makes me sleep worse.
dbas_items.reframe: You're already seeing the loop — that itself is the way out. Decouple sleep from worry: park tonight's worries for tomorrow (the worry box), so the bed becomes associated only with rest.
dbas_items.socratic_question: What you're worrying about — does it have to be solved right now, or can it move to a designated 'worry time' tomorrow?

dbas_items.belief: Insomnia is ruining my whole life.
dbas_items.reframe: Insomnia makes life harder, but 'ruining' is all-or-nothing. Place it back in proportion: which things this week were actually affected? Which weren't?
dbas_items.socratic_question: Six months from now, will insomnia be the thing that 'ruined your life' — or the moment you started learning to take care of yourself?

dbas_items.belief: I have to try hard to fall asleep, or insomnia wins.
dbas_items.reframe: Sleep is allowed, not forced. 'I must sleep' is one of the central maintainers of insomnia (stimulus-control therapy specifically targets breaking this link).
dbas_items.socratic_question: On the nights you tried hardest to sleep, were they better — or worse?
